2.6.2. Kiwifruit
      Kiwifruit are nutritionally dense containing a range of nutrients that can benefit sleep, health and
recovery including serotonin, vitamin C, vitamin E, vitamin K, folate, anthocyanidins, carotenoids,
beta-carotene, lutein, potassium, copper and fibre [70]. Interest in the antioxidant capacity, enzyme,
polyphenolic and phytochemical content of kiwifruit has increased steadily over the last decade [70–72].
It has been suggested that the various bioactive components in kiwifruit may act synergistically
affecting various physiological and metabolic processes (e.g., inhibition of oxidative and inflammatory
responses, improved gastrointestinal tract health and bowel function) [73]. Contemporary research
has focused on the health benefits of kiwifruit particularly in relation to antioxidant capacity, digestion,
iron nutrition, metabolic health and immune function [73].
      Regular consumption of kiwifruit has been found to significantly (p ≤ 0.05) increase plasma vitamin
C [74] vitamin E [71] and lutein/zeaxanthin concentrations [71,74]. A study involving volunteers (n = 25)
with a self-reported sleep disturbance demonstrated consumption of two kiwifruit one hour before
bedtime for four weeks significantly improved actigraphy-measured total sleep duration (+16.9%,
baseline 354.5 ± 17.1 min; post-intervention 395.3 ± 17.4 min) and sleep efficiency (+2.4%, baseline
93.9 ± 1.03 min; post-intervention 95.9 ± 0.67 min) (p ≤ 0.005) [70]. Self-report measures also improved
significantly, wake after sleep onset reduced (time awake during sleep period) (–28.9%), sleep onset
latency reduced (–35.4%) while sleep efficiency increased (5.4%) (p ≤ 0.002) [70]. Sleep quality was
significantly improved following the four-week kiwifruit intervention however, the lack of a control
group must be noted and there was a high level of subject drop out (n = 5). The findings may be prone
to bias as subjects were recruited based on interest in participation in a dietary intervention study
relating to sleep.
      Serotonin is the end product of L-tryptophan metabolism and is related to REM [70]. The serotonin
content in kiwifruit may contribute to improved sleep while the rich antioxidant content may supress
free radical expression and inflammatory cytokines. Folate deficiency has been linked to insomnia
(difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep, extended periods of wakefulness and/or insufficient sleep)
and restless leg syndrome (repeated movement of or undesirable sensations in legs leading to sleep
disruption) [70], the high folate content in kiwifruit may improve folate status and consequently
improve sleep [70]. Although folates are widely consumed in the diet, they are destroyed by cooking or
processing, however, kiwifruit are typically consumed in their raw form. Further research is warranted
within athletic populations to investigate the potential sleep promoting properties of kiwifruit and the
effect of kiwifruit consumption on both sleep quality, sleep quantity and recovery.

2.7. B Vitamins and Magnesium
      Vitamin B12 contributes to melatonin secretion, pyridoxine (vitamin B6 ) is involved in the
synthesis of serotonin from tryptophan and niacin (vitamin B3 ) may elicit a tryptophan sparing
effect [40]. Niacin can be synthesised endogenously from tryptophan via the Kynurenine Pathway,
therefore, consuming a sufficient amount of niacin is necessary to inhibit 2,3-dioxygenase activity
eliciting a tryptophan sparing effect, increasing its availability for synthesis serotonin and melatonin [40].
Folate (vitamin B9 ) and pyridoxine are involved in the conversion of tryptophan into serotonin [45].
The reduced form of folate (5-methyltetratrahydrofolate) increases tetrahydrobiopterin is a co-enzyme
of tryptophan-5-hydroxylase which converts tryptophan into 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT) [45].
Pyridoxine’s role in the conversion of tryptophan into serotonin is related to the amino acid
decarboxylase which speeds up the conversion rate of 5-HT to serotonin [45]. Mixed effects have
been observed, with different doses of cobalamin (vitamin B12 ) on sleep-wake rhythms and delayed
sleep phase syndrome (a significant delay in circadian rhythm), while no effect was observed for sleep
duration [41].
      Magnesium is also believed to enhance melatonin secretion promoting sleep onset and act as
a GABA agonist, the main inhibitory neurotransmitter that acts on the CNS [40]. Magnesium
is important for the production of the enzyme N-acetyltransferase which converts 5-HT into

N-acetyl-5-hydroxytryptamine, which can then be converted to melatonin [44]. A placebo controlled
double blind study on older adults (n = 43), demonstrated a food based supplement containing 5 mg
melatonin, 225 mg magnesium and 11.25 mg zinc, significantly (p < 0.001) improved subjective sleep
quality scores in the intervention group but not the controls (difference between the groups 6.8; 95%
CI 5.4–8.3) and total sleep duration (182.18 min; 95% CI 160.02–204.34) assessed via actigraphy [75].
The effects were attributed to the synergy between magnesium, zinc and melatonin [75]. It must be
noted that supplementing these nutrients will most likely only have an effect in cases of deficiency
or insufficiency.

3. Conclusions
     Nutrients such as antioxidants, tryptophan rich protein, carbohydrate, melatonin, micronutrients
and fruit can affect sleep [37,39,40]. Sleep can be promoted either by inhibiting wake-promoting
mechanisms or by increasing sleep promoting factors through nutritional interventions [40]. Based
on this review of the existing scientific literature, there appears to be considerable scope for
further investigation of nutrition interventions designed to enhance sleep quality and quantity
or promote general health, sleep health, training adaptations and/or recovery in both general and
athletic populations.

28	 "evidenceSummary": "Narrative review and international expert consensus (British Journal of Sports Medicine, 2020, online first) on sleep inadequacy and performance in elite athletes. It covers measurement tools, travel and jet lag, caffeine and nutrition, and sets out a practitioner sleep toolbox with five recommendations. The paper reports no new primary data.",
29	 "screeningLimitations": "Expert consensus with no described systematic search, so the evidence base and the weight given to each study cannot be checked. The authors themselves note that much sleep and performance research is of poor quality, with few female athletes and few controlled trials.",
30	 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could treat the toolbox and sleep-banking advice as proven performance interventions, when the authors say the evidence for sleep extension and napping is limited and mostly lacks controls.",
31	 "paper": {
32	  "year": 2020,
33	  "citation": "Walsh NP, Halson SL, Sargent C, Roach GD, Nedelec M, Gupta L, et al. Sleep and the athlete: narrative review and 2021 expert consensus recommendations. Br J Sports Med. 2020;0:1-13 (online first).",
34	  "doi": "10.1136/bjsports-2020-102025",
35	  "abstract": "Elite athletes are susceptible to sleep inadequacy, characterised by habitual sleep under 7 hours and poor sleep quality. Performance falls after a night or more without sleep, but the effect of partial restriction over one to three nights is unclear. The panel reviews the evidence, notes weaknesses in the research (poor control, few female athletes, weak sleep measures), and provides a practical sleep toolbox for practitioners.",
36	  "tldr": "Elite athletes often sleep under 7 hours and sleep poorly, mainly because of training, travel and competition schedules. Screen for sleep problems, educate athletes, and use naps and sleep planning where schedules limit night sleep.",
37	  "methods": "Narrative review by an international expert panel with a consensus process. The panel's selection and voting method is not described in the text. Topics include sleep measurement tools (Table 1), sleep and performance, sport-specific and general risk factors, travel and jet lag, nutrition and caffeine, and a practitioner toolbox.",
38	  "findings": "A night or more without sleep has a detrimental effect on sport-specific and physical performance, while the effect of partial restriction over one to three nights is mixed. Sleep disturbance affects 50% to 78% of elite athletes, and 22% to 26% have highly disturbed sleep. Caffeine typically increases sleep onset latency and reduces sleep duration and efficiency. Naps of 20 to 30 minutes improved sprint and peak jump velocity in cited studies. Sleep education sessions increased sleep duration by an average of 20 to 90 minutes, but the gains were not maintained at one-month follow-up.",
39	  "limitations": "The authors state that the quality of sleep and athletic performance research is poor, with inconsistent, unreliable and invalid methods, few female athletes and few controlled trials. Several sleep-extension findings come from studies without control groups, so parts of the toolbox rest on expert judgement.",
40	  "practicalImplications": "Screen athletes for sleep problems with a validated questionnaire and refer those with moderate or severe problems to a sleep specialist. Educate athletes about sleep, use naps under 30 minutes (or a 15 to 20 minute mid-afternoon coffee nap) to cover short nights, and limit caffeine, alcohol and heavy meals close to bedtime. Use sleep monitors with care, since they can increase worry about sleep.",
41	  "athleteDev": "Schedule training and travel to protect sleep, plan naps when night sleep is short, and use caffeine with care because it delays sleep onset and shortens sleep. Sleep banking before a key competition is an option for individual athletes, not a universal rule.",
42	  "rtp": "The paper addresses sleep in elite athletes in general and does not cover injured athletes or return-to-sport decisions. It cannot be used to set return-to-play criteria."
43	 }

     Sleep Architecture in Response to a Late Evening Competition
                         in Team-Sport Athletes
                       Jacopo Antonino Vitale, Andrea Galbiati, Gaia De Giacomi, Davide Tornese,
                             Daniel Levendowski, Luigi Ferini-Strambi, and Giuseppe Banﬁ

     Purpose: The aim of this study was to assess the effect of a late evening competition on sleep characteristics and perceived
     recovery in team-sport players using a validated self-applicable and portable polysomnographic device. Methods: Sixteen team-
     sport players (age: 25.4 [1.4] y; body mass index: 23.6 [0.5] kg/m2) completed the study. Objective and subjective sleep data were
     collected for 4 consecutive nights: 2 nights before (PRE2 and PRE1) and the 2 nights after an evening match (POST1), performed
     between 6:00 PM and 9:00 PM. Total quality of recovery values were also collected in the morning. Results: A signiﬁcantly
     delayed bedtime (P < .0001; η2p = .68, large) was observed in the ﬁrst night after the competition (2 h 29 min [1 h 15 min])
     compared both to PRE2 (+88 min; P < .0001), PRE1 (+98 min; P < .0001), and POST1 (+100 min; P < .0001), and similar results
     were observed for wake-up time (P = .033; η2p = .39, large): Players woke up signiﬁcantly later in evening match (9 h 20 min [1 h
     55 min]) compared with PRE2 (+85 min; P = .050) and POST1 (+85 min; P = .049). Conversely, total sleep time; sleep
     efﬁciency; sleep onset latency; wake after sleep onset; cortical arousals; N1, N2, N3, and REM (rapid eye movement)
     percentages; total quality of recovery values; and scores of subjective sleep quality did not vary among the 4 study nights.
     Conclusions: Team-sport players had delayed bedtime and wake-up time following an evening competition; however, sleep
     quality, duration, and subjective scores of recovery were not affected by the evening match. The delayed wake-up time seems to
     protect athletes’ sleep efﬁciency/duration against the evening-match-induced delayed bedtime.

     Keywords: REM, sleep quality, time of day, evening match

    ABSTRACT                                                                                                                                                 KEYWORDS
    Field-based athlete research has primarily focused on sleep-wake patterns, but technological advance­                                                    Sleep architecture; travel;
    ments now enable detailed assessment of sleep architecture. This study compared sleep quantity, quality,                                                 rugby; team-sport; athletes;
    and architecture during home (no travel; HOME) and away (eastbound travel across three time zones;                                                       polysomnography
    AWAY) matches in professional male rugby union. The sleep of twenty athletes was assessed using home-
    based polysomnography over three nights per condition: two nights preceding the match (MD-2), match
    night (MD), and the following night after (MD + 1). Sleep duration, efficiency, onset/offset, latency, wake
    after sleep onset, awakenings, and sleep stages (as light, deep and rapid eye movement [REM] sleep,
    evaluated as proportion [%] and time [min]) were monitored. Compared to HOME, AWAY increased sleep
    onset latency (+12 ± 23 min; p < 0.01) and reduced light sleep (−6.2 ± 7.1%; p < 0.01). Match days (MD)
    incurred delayed bedtime (+71 ± 135 min; p < 0.001), reduced sleep duration (−94 ± 120 min; p < 0.05),
    and altered sleep architecture (deep: +9.8 ± 10.0%; REM: −6.9 ± 8.3%; both p < 0.05) compared to MD-2.
    On MD + 1, sleep duration (+96 ± 147 min; p < 0.01) and light and REM sleep time rebounded (+52 ±
    44 min and + 39 ± 52 min, respectively; both p < 0.05). Travel and matches altered sleep architecture in
    professional rugby. Training and flight schedules should ensure sufficient sleep opportunity after travel
    and matchday to optimise recovery.

Tests were the ImPACT battery, the Post-Concussion Symptom Scale (PCSS), and paper-and-pencil and computerised neuropsychological measures, converted to z-scores from published norms. Aim 1 compared baseline athletes sleeping 5.78 hours or less (n=100) with those sleeping more than 7.07 hours (n=508). Aim 2: overall symptoms and most clusters did not differ between short-sleep baseline athletes and sufficient-sleep post-concussion athletes. 24	            negative health outcomes, including worse cognition. As such, the current study sought to examine the relationship
25	            between sleep difficulties and self-reported symptoms and objective neuropsychological performance at baseline and
26	            post-concussion in collegiate athletes. Method: Seven hundred seventy-two collegiate athletes completed a
27	            comprehensive neuropsychological test battery at baseline and/or post-concussion. Athletes were separated into two
28	            groups based on the amount of sleep the night prior to testing. The sleep duration cutoffs for these group were
29	            empirically determined by sample mean and standard deviation (M = 7.07, SD = 1.29). Results: Compared with athletes
30	            getting sufficient sleep, those getting insufficient sleep the night prior to baseline reported significantly more overall
31	            symptoms and more symptoms from each of the five symptom clusters of the Post-Concussion Symptom Scale.
32	            However, there were no significant differences on objective performance indices. Secondly, there were no significant
33	            differences on any of the outcome measures, except for sleep symptoms and headache, between athletes getting
34	            insufficient sleep at baseline and those getting sufficient sleep post-concussion. Conclusion: Overall, the effect of
35	            insufficient sleep at baseline can make an athlete appear similar to a concussed athlete with sufficient sleep. As such,
36	            athletes completing a baseline assessment following insufficient sleep could be underperforming cognitively and
37	            reporting elevated symptoms that would skew post-concussion comparisons. Therefore, there may need to be
38	            consideration of prior night’s sleep when determining whether a baseline can be used as a valid comparison.

            Sleep Deprived or Concussed? The Acute Impact of Self-Reported
            Insufficient Sleep in College Athletes



            Kaitlin E. Riegler*             Erin T. Guty           , Garrett A. Thomas and Peter A. Arnett
            Department of Psychology, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA 16802, USA

            (RECEIVED January 20, 2020; FINAL REVISION May 15, 2020; ACCEPTED May 19, 2020; FIRST PUBLISHED ONLINE July 9, 2020)




            Abstract

            Objective: Sleep deprivation is common among both college students and athletes and has been correlated with
            negative health outcomes, including worse cognition. As such, the current study sought to examine the relationship
            between sleep difficulties and self-reported symptoms and objective neuropsychological performance at baseline and
            post-concussion in collegiate athletes. Method: Seven hundred seventy-two collegiate athletes completed a
            comprehensive neuropsychological test battery at baseline and/or post-concussion. Athletes were separated into two
            groups based on the amount of sleep the night prior to testing. The sleep duration cutoffs for these group were
            empirically determined by sample mean and standard deviation (M = 7.07, SD = 1.29). Results: Compared with athletes
            getting sufficient sleep, those getting insufficient sleep the night prior to baseline reported significantly more overall
            symptoms and more symptoms from each of the five symptom clusters of the Post-Concussion Symptom Scale.
            However, there were no significant differences on objective performance indices. Secondly, there were no significant
            differences on any of the outcome measures, except for sleep symptoms and headache, between athletes getting
            insufficient sleep at baseline and those getting sufficient sleep post-concussion. Conclusion: Overall, the effect of
            insufficient sleep at baseline can make an athlete appear similar to a concussed athlete with sufficient sleep. As such,
            athletes completing a baseline assessment following insufficient sleep could be underperforming cognitively and
            reporting elevated symptoms that would skew post-concussion comparisons. Therefore, there may need to be
            consideration of prior night’s sleep when determining whether a baseline can be used as a valid comparison.
            Keywords: Cognition function, Post-concussion symptoms, Concussion, Mild, Sports injuries, Self report, Sports

At least mild sleep-disordered breathing (RDI of 5 or more) was found in 19% (95% CI 12.8% to 26.6%), and 4.4% had an RDI of 15 or more. Linemen and non-linemen did not differ in prevalence or severity, and SDB was not well correlated with blood pressure or metabolic measures.",
28	 "screeningLimitations": "Players who agreed to testing reported louder snoring than those who declined, so prevalence may be biased. Of 159 players, 22 had under two hours of usable data. Single-channel airflow monitoring at home, the lack of a control group, and comparisons with polysomnography data from other populations limit precision. Data were collected in 2007.",
29	 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the abstract's statement that SDB was positively associated with adiposity as a confirmed link, when every anthropometric association in Table 3 was small and not statistically significant.",
30	 "paper": {
31	  "year": 2010,
32	  "citation": "Rice TB, Dunn RE, Lincoln AE, Tucker AM, Vogel RA, Heyer RA, et al. Sleep-disordered breathing in the National Football League. Sleep. 2010;33(6):819-824.",
33	  "doi": "",
34	  "abstract": "Study objectives: to estimate the prevalence of sleep-disordered breathing (SDB) among NFL players and its associations with anthropometric measures and cardiovascular risk factors. Design: cross-sectional cohort. Participants: 137 active veteran players from six NFL teams. Results: mean RDI 4.7; 19% had at least mild SDB (RDI of 5 or more) and 4.4% had an RDI of 15 or more; linemen and non-linemen did not differ; no single anthropometric measure was highly associated with SDB, and SDB was not well correlated with cardiovascular risk factors. Conclusions: SDB was modest, mostly mild, positively associated with several measures of adiposity, and did not account for excess cardiovascular risk.",
35	  "tldr": "About one in five active NFL veterans had at least mild sleep apnoea on a home test, and fewer than one in twenty had moderate or severe disease. SDB did not explain the high blood pressure seen in these players.",
36	  "methods": "Cross-sectional sleep substudy of a cardiovascular evaluation of active NFL veterans, conducted at team mini-camps from April to July 2007. Of 159 players who agreed to home monitoring, 137 had at least two hours of data. An ApneaLink single-channel airflow monitor provided the respiratory disturbance index (RDI). Anthropometric and cardiovascular measures were taken at the same visit, and regression models were adjusted for age and race.",
37	  "findings": "Mean RDI was 4.7 (SD 12) and median 2. At least mild SDB (RDI of 5 or more) was present in 19% (95% CI 12.8% to 26.6%) and RDI of 15 or more in 4.4% (95% CI 1.6% to 9.2%). Linemen and non-linemen did not differ. In the adjusted linear models (Table 3), no anthropometric measure was significantly associated with RDI (P from 0.11 to 0.80). SDB was not associated with systolic blood pressure or hypertension, and it was not well correlated with fasting glucose or lipid measures.",
38	  "limitations": "The sample was biased toward players who reported significant snoring. Missing or short recordings (22 of 159) and airflow-only scoring, which may under-count hypopneas without a desaturation threshold, add imprecision. The authors state the study was underpowered for full analysis and had no control group, and comparisons with other populations use polysomnography, so they are not like-for-like. Conflict to note: the abstract says SDB was positively associated with several measures of adiposity, but no association in Table 3 reached significance.",
39	  "practicalImplications": "Sleep apnoea was less common in these players than their body size might suggest, but it was still present in about one in five. Screening players who are large or snore loudly for sleep-disordered breathing is reasonable. Weight and blood pressure should be managed directly, because the authors found SDB did not explain the high blood pressure.",
40	  "athleteDev": "The study does not address performance. For development staff, it suggests asking heavier players about snoring and sleepiness as part of routine screening, since mild sleep-disordered breathing was common in this group.",
41	  "rtp": "The study does not address injury or return to sport and gives no return-to-play information. It cannot inform return-to-play decisions."

14	    Study Objectives: Prior studies have suggested that the prevalence of sleep disordered breathing (SDB) among players in the National Football
15	    League (NFL) is disproportionately high. SDB can increase cardiovascular disease risk and is correlated with hypertension. NFL players have a
16	    higher prevalence of hypertension, and we sought to determine the prevalence of SDB among players the NFL and the associations of SDB with
17	    anthropometric measures and cardiovascular risk factors.
18	    Design: Cross-sectional cohort study.
19	    Setting: NFL athletic training facilities from April to July 2007.
20	    Participants: A total of 137 active veteran players from 6 NFL teams.
21	    Measurements: This evaluation of SDB among players in the NFL used a single-channel, home-based, unattended, portable, sleep apnea monitor.
22	    Multiple domains of self-reported sleep were assessed. Weight, body mass index, body fat percentage, neck circumference, waist circumference,
23	    and waist-to-hip ratio, as well as blood pressure, cholesterol, and fasting glucose concentrations were measured.
24	    Results: The mean respiratory disturbance index was 4.7 (± 12), with a median (interquartile range) of 2 (1,4). The prevalence of at least mild
25	    SDB (RDI ≥ 5) was 19% (95% confidence interval, 12.8%-26.6%). Only 4.4% (95% confidence interval, 1.6%-9.2%) of participants had respiratory
26	    disturbance index of 15 or greater. Linemen and non-linemen were not different in their prevalence or severity of SDB. No single anthropometric
27	    measure was highly associated with SDB, and SDB was not well correlated with cardiovascular risk factors.
28	    Conclusions: The prevalence of SDB in active NFL players was modest, predominately mild, and positively associated with several measures of
29	    adiposity. SDB did not account for excess cardiovascular risk factors.

SLEEP-DISORDERED BREATHING IN THE NFL

Sleep-Disordered Breathing in the National Football League
Thomas B. Rice, MD1; Reginald E. Dunn, BA4; Andrew E. Lincoln, ScD4; Andrew M. Tucker, MD5; Robert A. Vogel, MD6; Robert A. Heyer, MD7;
Anthony P. Yates, MD1; Peter W. F. Wilson, MD, MPH8; Elliot J. Pellmen, MD9; Thomas W. Allen, DO10; Anne B. Newman, MD, MPH1,3; Patrick J. Strollo, Jr., MD1,2
For the National Football League Subcommittee on Cardiovascular Health
1
 Department of Medicine, 2Clinical Translational Science Institute and 3Department of Epidemiology, University of Pittsburgh, Pittsburgh, PA; 4Sports
Medicine Research Center, Medstar Research Institute, 5Union Memorial Sports Medicine, Union Memorial Hospital, and 6Department of Cardiology,
University of Maryland School of Medicine, Baltimore MD; 7Department of Medicine, Carolinas Medical Center, Charlotte, NC; 8Department of Medicine,
Emory University School of Medicine, Atlanta, GA; 9ProHEALTH Care Associates, Lake Success, and Departments of Medicine and Orthopaedics, Mount
Sinai School of Medicine, New York, NY; 10Department of Sports/Family Medicine, University of Oklahoma College of Medicine, Tulsa, OK

    Study Objectives: Prior studies have suggested that the prevalence of sleep disordered breathing (SDB) among players in the National Football
    League (NFL) is disproportionately high. SDB can increase cardiovascular disease risk and is correlated with hypertension. NFL players have a
    higher prevalence of hypertension, and we sought to determine the prevalence of SDB among players the NFL and the associations of SDB with
    anthropometric measures and cardiovascular risk factors.
    Design: Cross-sectional cohort study.
    Setting: NFL athletic training facilities from April to July 2007.
    Participants: A total of 137 active veteran players from 6 NFL teams.
    Measurements: This evaluation of SDB among players in the NFL used a single-channel, home-based, unattended, portable, sleep apnea monitor.
    Multiple domains of self-reported sleep were assessed. Weight, body mass index, body fat percentage, neck circumference, waist circumference,
    and waist-to-hip ratio, as well as blood pressure, cholesterol, and fasting glucose concentrations were measured.
    Results: The mean respiratory disturbance index was 4.7 (± 12), with a median (interquartile range) of 2 (1,4). The prevalence of at least mild
    SDB (RDI ≥ 5) was 19% (95% confidence interval, 12.8%-26.6%). Only 4.4% (95% confidence interval, 1.6%-9.2%) of participants had respiratory
    disturbance index of 15 or greater. Linemen and non-linemen were not different in their prevalence or severity of SDB. No single anthropometric
    measure was highly associated with SDB, and SDB was not well correlated with cardiovascular risk factors.
    Conclusions: The prevalence of SDB in active NFL players was modest, predominately mild, and positively associated with several measures of
    adiposity. SDB did not account for excess cardiovascular risk factors.
    Keywords: Sleep disordered breathing, sleep apnea, obesity, National Football League, cardiovascular risk
    Citation: Rice TB; Dunn RE; Lincoln AE; Tucker AM; Vogel RA; Heyer RA; Yates AP; Wilson PWF; Pellmen EJ; Allen TW; Newman AB; Strollo PJ.
    Sleep-disordered breathing in the National Football League. SLEEP 2010;33(6):819-824.

{
 "id": "Q65",
 "sourceFile": "Sleep and nutrition interactions -   Implications for athletes.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title 'Sleep and Nutrition Interactions: Implications for Athletes' in the text matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Narrative Review",
 "primaryDomain": "Nutrition & Hydration",
 "domains": [
  "Nutrition & Hydration",
  "Recovery & Readiness"
 ],
 "audiences": [
  "Nutrition",
  "Performance"
 ],
 "sports": [
  "Mixed / General Sport"
 ],
 "populations": [
  "Mixed / Unspecified"
 ],
 "evidenceSummary": "Narrative review (Nutrients, 2019) of how sleep and nutrition interact, with athletes as the target group. It reports sleep effects of high glycaemic index evening carbohydrate, tart cherry juice, kiwifruit, melatonin and tryptophan-rich protein, drawn from quoted trials that mostly enrolled healthy adults or people with sleep complaints. It reports no new data.",
 "screeningLimitations": "No search strategy or evidence grading is described, so study selection cannot be reproduced. The cited sleep trials are small, several have no control group, and few included athletes.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the listed foods and nutrients as proven sleep aids for athletes, when the review says athlete-specific evidence is lacking.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2019,
  "citation": "Doherty R, Madigan S, Warrington G, Ellis J. Sleep and Nutrition Interactions: Implications for Athletes. Nutrients. 2019;11:822.",
  "doi": "10.3390/nu11040822",
  "abstract": "This narrative review explores the relationship between sleep and nutrition. Various nutritional interventions have been shown to improve sleep, including high carbohydrate, high glycaemic index evening meals, melatonin, tryptophan-rich protein, tart cherry juice, kiwifruit and micronutrients. The authors state that functional food-based interventions designed to enhance sleep and recovery warrant further investigation.",
  "tldr": "Several foods and nutrients have improved sleep in small studies, mostly outside athletic groups. For athletes they are options to test, not proven interventions.",
  "methods": "Narrative review with no described search strategy. It covers sleep physiology, the sleep-nutrition link and specific nutrients: carbohydrate, melatonin, tryptophan-rich protein, antioxidants, tart cherry, kiwifruit, B vitamins and magnesium.",
  "findings": "In one study, a high glycaemic index meal eaten four hours before bed cut sleep onset latency to 9.0 min, against 17.5 min after a low glycaemic index meal. In one study of healthy adults, tart cherry juice increased total sleep time by 34 min. In 25 volunteers with sleep disturbance, two kiwifruit an hour before bed for four weeks increased actigraphy sleep duration by 16.9%, with no control group. In six healthy men, melatonin at 0.3 mg or 1 mg shortened sleep onset latency when taken at 6 pm or 8 pm, but 0.3 mg taken at 9 pm lengthened it.",
  "limitations": "No systematic search or quality appraisal is described. Several cited trials are small or uncontrolled. The review notes that most antioxidant studies have been done in healthy adults, and that a melatonin, magnesium and zinc supplement will most likely only help where there is a deficiency or insufficiency.",
  "practicalImplications": "Evening meal timing and content are low-risk options to test with athletes who struggle to fall asleep. Late caffeine and alcohol are reasonable to limit, given their documented effects on sleep onset, duration and REM sleep. Magnesium and zinc supplements are likely to help only where there is a deficiency, and any supplement should be checked for banned substances.",
  "athleteDev": "Use evening food timing and content, plus limits on late caffeine and alcohol, as first sleep steps for athletes. Treat tart cherry, kiwifruit and tryptophan-rich protein as options to trial and track with individual athletes, not as proven interventions.",
  "rtp": "The review does not address injured athletes or return to sport, and its sleep findings come mostly from non-athletes. It should not guide return-to-sport decisions."
 },
 "verification": {
  "status": "CORRECTED",
  "changes": [
   "paper.limitations: said most 'antioxidant and sleep work' was in healthy adults -> limited to antioxidant studies, as the text states ('the majority of studies have been conducted on healthy adults' in the antioxidant section); deficiency caveat tied to the melatonin, magnesium and zinc supplement it refers to",
   "paper.practicalImplications: said melatonin supplements are unlikely to help athletes without a deficiency, which contradicts the review's melatonin section ('low dose of melatonin ... can elicit a sleep-inducing effect') -> deficiency caveat now limited to magnesium and zinc"
  ],
  "residualConcerns": "",
  "spotCheckPriority": "normal"
 }
}

It also notes that poor sleep the night before neurocognitive testing can raise symptom scores and impede return to play.",

 "decision": "INCLUDE",

 ],

 ],
 "evidenceSummary": "Narrative review and international expert consensus (British Journal of Sports Medicine, 2020, online first) on sleep inadequacy and performance in elite athletes. It covers measurement tools, travel and jet lag, caffeine and nutrition, gives five key recommendations on sleep and performance, and sets out a four-tool practitioner sleep toolbox (education, screening, naps, banking sleep). The paper reports no new primary data.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Expert consensus with no described systematic search, so the evidence base and the weight given to each study cannot be checked. The authors themselves note that much sleep and performance research is of poor quality, with few female athletes and few controlled trials.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could treat the toolbox and sleep-banking advice as proven performance interventions, when the authors say research is still needed on napping and sleep extension and that sleep-extension studies often lack objective sleep measures or a control group.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2020,
  "citation": "Walsh NP, Halson SL, Sargent C, Roach GD, Nedelec M, Gupta L, et al. Sleep and the athlete: narrative review and 2021 expert consensus recommendations. Br J Sports Med. 2020 (published online 3 November 2020).",
  "doi": "10.1136/bjsports-2020-102025",
  "abstract": "Elite athletes are susceptible to sleep inadequacy, characterised by habitual sleep under 7 hours and poor sleep quality. Performance falls after a night or more without sleep, but the effect of partial restriction over one to three nights is unclear. The panel reviews the evidence, notes weaknesses in the research (poor control, few female athletes, weak sleep measures), and provides a practical sleep toolbox for practitioners.",
  "tldr": "Elite athletes often sleep under 7 hours and sleep poorly, mainly because of training, travel and competition schedules. Screen for sleep problems, educate athletes, and use naps and sleep planning where schedules limit night sleep.",
  "methods": "Narrative review by an international expert panel with a consensus process. The panel's selection and voting method is not described in the text. Topics include sleep measurement tools (Table 1), sleep and performance, sport-specific and general risk factors, travel and jet lag, nutrition and caffeine, and a practitioner toolbox.",
  "findings": "A night or more without sleep has a detrimental effect on sport-specific and physical performance, while the effect of partial restriction over one to three nights is mixed. Sleep disturbance affects 50% to 78% of elite athletes, and 22% to 26% have highly disturbed sleep. Caffeine typically increases sleep onset latency and reduces sleep duration and efficiency. Naps of 20 to 30 minutes improved sprint and peak jump velocity in cited studies. Sleep education sessions of 30 to 60 minutes increased sleep duration by an average of 20 to 90 minutes, but in one study the gains were not maintained at one-month follow-up.",
  "limitations": "The authors state that the quality of sleep and athletic performance research is poor, with inconsistent, unreliable and invalid methods, few female athletes and few controlled trials. Several sleep-extension findings come from studies without control groups, so parts of the toolbox rest on expert judgement.",
  "practicalImplications": "Screen athletes for sleep problems with a validated questionnaire and refer those with moderate or severe problems to a sleep specialist. Educate athletes about sleep, use naps under 30 minutes (or a 15 to 20 minute mid-afternoon coffee nap) to cover short nights, and limit caffeine, alcohol and heavy meals close to bedtime. Use sleep monitors with care, since they can increase worry about sleep.",
  "athleteDev": "Schedule training and travel to protect sleep, plan naps when night sleep is short, and use caffeine with care because it delays sleep onset and shortens sleep. Sleep banking before a key competition is an option for individual athletes, not a universal rule.",
  "rtp": "The paper addresses sleep in elite athletes in general and does not cover injured athletes or return-to-sport decisions. It cannot be used to set return-to-play criteria."
 },

   "evidenceSummary: said the toolbox had five recommendations -> the five recommendations are Box 1 on sleep and performance; the toolbox (Box 2) has four tools ('Tool #1' to 'Tool #4')",

  ],

  "spotCheckPriority": "normal"
 }
}

{
 "id": "Q68",
 "sourceFile": "Sleep architecture in response to a late evening competition in team-sport athletes.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title 'Sleep Architecture in Response to a Late Evening Competition in Team-Sport Athletes' in the text matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Cohort Study",
 "primaryDomain": "Recovery & Readiness",
 "domains": [
  "Recovery & Readiness",
  "Training & Performance"
 ],
 "audiences": [
  "Performance",
  "Athletic Training"
 ],
 "sports": [
  "Volleyball",
  "Basketball",
  "Other Sport"
 ],
 "populations": [
  "Male Athletes",
  "Healthy Athletes",
  "Mixed / Unspecified"
 ],
 "evidenceSummary": "Observational study (International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance, 2022) in 16 male team-sport players (field hockey, volleyball, basketball) who wore a portable polysomnography device for four nights: two before and two after an evening match. Within the group, bedtime was about 90 to 100 minutes later on the night after the match, and wake-up was later, but total sleep time, sleep efficiency, sleep stages and recovery scores did not change significantly.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Small sample: 16 analysed of 25 eligible, from three sports at regional and national level, with a single match and no control group. Caffeine, alcohol, napping and screen use were not controlled, and non-significant results with n=16 do not show that there is no effect.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the unchanged sleep duration and quality as evidence that evening matches do not harm sleep, when the same study found a later bedtime and later wake-up.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2022,
  "citation": "Vitale JA, Galbiati A, De Giacomi G, Tornese D, Levendowski D, Ferini-Strambi L, et al. Sleep architecture in response to a late evening competition in team-sport athletes. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2022;17(4):569-575.",
  "doi": "10.1123/ijspp.2021-0292",
  "abstract": "Purpose: to assess the effect of a late evening competition on sleep characteristics and perceived recovery in team-sport players using a validated portable polysomnographic device. Methods: sixteen players recorded sleep for four consecutive nights, two before and two after an evening match played between 6:00 and 9:00 pm. Results: bedtime on the first night after the match (mean 02:29) was 88 to 100 minutes later than on the other nights, and wake-up was later, while total sleep time, sleep efficiency, sleep onset latency, WASO, arousals, sleep stages, recovery and subjective sleep quality did not differ across nights. Conclusions: the later wake-up seemed to protect sleep efficiency and duration against the later bedtime.",
  "tldr": "After a late evening match, these players went to bed and woke up later, but total sleep, sleep efficiency and recovery scores did not change. The later wake-up appeared to offset the later bedtime.",
  "methods": "Observational study over four nights (two before and two after an evening match at 6 to 9 pm) in 16 male players from field hockey, volleyball and basketball. Sleep was recorded with a portable forehead device that provides EEG-based sleep staging, alongside sleep diaries and the Total Quality Recovery scale. Repeated-measures ANOVA or Friedman tests were used.",
  "findings": "Bedtime was about 88 to 100 minutes later on the first night after the match than on the two pre-match nights and the second post-match night (P < .0001). Wake-up time was about 85 minutes later than on two of the other nights (P = .049 to .050). Total sleep time was about 6.0 hours after the match and did not differ between nights (P = .253). Sleep efficiency, sleep stages, arousals, sleep quality and recovery scores did not change significantly.",
  "limitations": "Sixteen men from three sports at regional and national level. The authors note that the sample was small and that sport and chronotype subgroups could not be compared. Only one match and four nights were recorded. The device was uncomfortable, which limits longer use, and lifestyle factors such as caffeine, alcohol and device use were not controlled.",
  "practicalImplications": "In these players a later bedtime after an evening match did not appear to harm sleep. The authors suggest that forcing players to bed straight after a match could be counterproductive, and that the morning after a night match should be free of training or social commitments so athletes can extend sleep.",
  "athleteDev": "Protect the morning after an evening match from early training or commitments so players can sleep later, and avoid forcing an early bedtime straight after the match. Track sleep across the nights around a match, since this study sampled one fixture.",
  "rtp": "The study is in healthy athletes during a competitive season and does not address injured athletes or return-to-sport decisions. It cannot inform return-to-sport timing."
 },
 "verification": {
  "status": "CORRECTED",
  "changes": [
   "paper.abstract: read the post-match bedtime '2 h 29 min' as a 2.5 h delay -> it is the mean clock time 02:29 (Table 1 'Bedtime ... 02:29 (01:15)'); the delay was +88 to +100 min",
   "paper.abstract: conclusion softened from 'protected' to 'seemed to protect', matching 'The delayed wake-up time seems to protect'"
  ],
  "residualConcerns": "",
  "spotCheckPriority": "normal"
 }
}

 "decision": "INCLUDE",

 "sports": [

 ],
 "populations": [
  "Professional / Elite",
  "Male Athletes"
 ],
 "evidenceSummary": "Prospective observational study (Journal of Sports Sciences, 2025) using home-based polysomnography in 20 male professional rugby union players over a home match and an away match involving eastbound travel. The match night had a later bedtime (+71 min), about 94 min less sleep, a higher deep-sleep proportion (+9.8%) and a lower REM proportion (-6.9%) than two nights before the match. The away condition had longer sleep onset latency (+12 min) and less light sleep (-6.2%) than the home condition, and total sleep rebounded by about 96 min the following night.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Only 69 of 120 planned nights were recorded, the condition order was fixed (home first), there was no night before the match (MD-1), and only one away trip in one season was studied. Sleep was staged manually by one scientist, and some players found the device uncomfortable.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the MD+1 rebound as full recovery. The authors warn that rebound sleep can mislead, because it can hide accumulated sleep debt and residual fatigue.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2025,
  "citation": "Uchiyama K, Peeling P, Halson SL, Reid M, Wallman K, Walsh J, et al. Sleep architecture is altered with travel and matches in professional rugby union players. J Sports Sci. 2025.",
  "doi": "10.1080/02640414.2025.2473150",
  "abstract": "This study compared sleep quantity, quality and architecture during home and away matches in professional male rugby union players. Twenty athletes had home-based polysomnography over three nights per condition: two before the match, the match night and the night after. Away travel (eastbound, three time zones) increased sleep onset latency and reduced light sleep. Match days delayed bedtime, reduced sleep duration and altered sleep architecture, with more deep and less REM sleep. Sleep duration, light sleep and REM sleep rebounded on the following night.",
  "tldr": "Matches and travel shortened and reshaped sleep in professional rugby players, with later bedtimes and less REM sleep on match nights and a partial rebound the next night. Plan sleep opportunity after travel and match days.",
  "methods": "Prospective observational study across the first two rounds of the 2023 Super Rugby Pacific season. Twenty players (age 27.5 +/- 4.1 years) wore a wireless home polysomnography device (Somfit) on three nights per fixture (MD-2, MD and MD+1). The away fixture involved a 3.6 h eastbound flight across three time zones. Linear mixed-effects models with Tukey-adjusted post hoc tests were used.",
  "findings": "Away compared with home: sleep onset latency was 12 min longer (P = .003) and light sleep proportion was 6.2% lower (P = .002). Match day compared with MD-2: bedtime was about 71 min later, total sleep time 94 min shorter (P = .016), deep sleep proportion 9.8% higher (P = .014) and REM proportion 6.9% lower (P = .026). On MD+1, total sleep rebounded by 96 min, and light and REM sleep rose by 52 and 39 min. Sleep efficiency did not differ by day or condition.",
  "limitations": "Conflict to note: the abstract gives the MD+1 light-sleep change as +52 +/- 44 min, while the Results text gives +/- 94 min; the mean is the same. The sample was small (69 of 120 planned nights), the design was non-randomised with home always first, there was no MD-1 night, and only one fixture pair was studied. The device was uncomfortable for some players, and sleep before the match was not measured.",
  "practicalImplications": "Plan sleep opportunity after away travel and match days. The authors suggest avoiding early return flights after an away match, creating dark, quiet and cool hotel rooms, and later training starts after travel. Read rebound sleep with caution, because it can hide accumulated sleep debt.",
  "athleteDev": "Protect sleep after travel and match days with later training starts, sleep-friendly hotel rooms and, where possible, no early-morning return flights. Read post-match rebound sleep in context, since the authors warn it can make players look recovered when residual fatigue remains.",
  "rtp": "The study looks at healthy players during the season and does not address injured athletes or return to sport. It cannot guide return-to-sport decisions."
 },
 "verification": {
  "status": "CORRECTED",
  "changes": [
   "paper.athleteDev: said the authors suggest tracking fatigue alongside sleep as practice -> the authors list fatigue markers as future research ('Future studies should include fatigue markers'); now framed as reading rebound sleep in context ('high-performance staff need to consider the context')"
  ],
  "residualConcerns": "The Methods define MD+1 as 'the second night following matchday', while the abstract calls it 'the following night after'; the timing of the rebound night is ambiguous in the source.",
  "spotCheckPriority": "high"
 }
}

 ],
 "evidenceSummary": "Cross-sectional study (Sleep, 2010) of 137 veteran NFL players from six teams who wore a single-channel home sleep apnoea monitor. At least mild sleep-disordered breathing (RDI of 5 or more) was found in 19% (95% CI 12.8% to 26.6%), and 4.4% had an RDI of 15 or more. Linemen and non-linemen did not differ in prevalence or severity, and SDB was not well correlated with blood pressure or metabolic measures.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Players who agreed to testing reported louder snoring than those who declined, so prevalence may be biased. Of 159 players, 22 had under two hours of usable data. Single-channel airflow monitoring at home, the lack of a control group, and comparisons with polysomnography data from other populations limit precision. Data were collected in 2007.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the abstract's statement that SDB was positively associated with adiposity as a confirmed link, when every anthropometric association in Table 3 was small and not statistically significant.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2010,
  "citation": "Rice TB, Dunn RE, Lincoln AE, Tucker AM, Vogel RA, Heyer RA, et al. Sleep-disordered breathing in the National Football League. Sleep. 2010;33(6):819-824.",
  "doi": "",
  "abstract": "Study objectives: to estimate the prevalence of sleep-disordered breathing (SDB) among NFL players and its associations with anthropometric measures and cardiovascular risk factors. Design: cross-sectional cohort. Participants: 137 active veteran players from six NFL teams. Results: mean RDI 4.7; 19% had at least mild SDB (RDI of 5 or more) and 4.4% had an RDI of 15 or more; linemen and non-linemen did not differ; no single anthropometric measure was highly associated with SDB, and SDB was not well correlated with cardiovascular risk factors. Conclusions: SDB was modest, mostly mild, positively associated with several measures of adiposity, and did not account for excess cardiovascular risk.",
  "tldr": "About one in five active NFL veterans had at least mild sleep apnoea on a home test, and fewer than one in twenty had moderate or severe disease. SDB did not explain the high blood pressure seen in these players.",
  "methods": "Cross-sectional sleep substudy of a cardiovascular evaluation of active NFL veterans, conducted at team mini-camps from April to July 2007. Of 159 players who agreed to home monitoring, 137 had at least two hours of data. An ApneaLink single-channel airflow monitor provided the respiratory disturbance index (RDI). Anthropometric and cardiovascular measures were taken at the same visit, and regression models were adjusted for age and race.",
  "findings": "Mean RDI was 4.7 (SD 12) and median 2. At least mild SDB (RDI of 5 or more) was present in 19% (95% CI 12.8% to 26.6%) and RDI of 15 or more in 4.4% (95% CI 1.6% to 9.2%). Linemen and non-linemen did not differ. In the adjusted linear models (Table 3), no anthropometric measure was significantly associated with RDI (P from 0.11 to 0.80). SDB was not associated with systolic blood pressure or hypertension, and it was not well correlated with fasting glucose or lipid measures.",
  "limitations": "The sample was biased toward players who reported significant snoring. Missing or short recordings (22 of 159) and airflow-only scoring, which may under-count hypopneas without a desaturation threshold, add imprecision. The authors state the study was underpowered for full analysis and had no control group, and comparisons with other populations use polysomnography, so they are not like-for-like. Conflict to note: the abstract says SDB was positively associated with several measures of adiposity, but no association in Table 3 reached significance.",
  "practicalImplications": "About one in five players had at least mild SDB, a prevalence the authors describe as in line with what the players' BMI would predict. Body size and snoring did not pick out affected players here: every player reported snoring, and linemen did not differ from non-linemen. The authors call for education and careful monitoring of weight and blood pressure, because SDB did not explain the high blood pressure.",
  "athleteDev": "The study does not address performance. It shows that mild SDB was common across positions in this group, so position or size alone should not be used to decide who might have it.",
  "rtp": "The study does not address injury or return to sport and gives no return-to-play information. It cannot inform return-to-play decisions."
 },
 "verification": {
  "status": "CORRECTED",
  "changes": [
   "paper.practicalImplications: said SDB was 'less common than their body size might suggest' -> the authors say prevalence 'appears to be in line with estimates of what would be predicted by the participants' BMI distribution'",

  "spotCheckPriority": "high"
 }
}
